Analysis.object: Our results demonstrate that obligatory runners differ from non-obligatory runners on athletic identity and levels of disordered eating.

One limitation of the current study was that all measures were self-report in nature. In previous studies, researchers have found that self-report measures regarding disordered eating tend to be associated with underreporting.

For the purpose of this study obligatory and non-obligatory runners were dichotomized. It is likely, however, that this form of exercise occurs on a continuum and it would be valuable to assess this. Longitudinal research of those at risk for becoming obligatory runners could determine whether the shift towards obligatory running patterns occurs immediately after adopting an exercise regimen or whether the change occurs over time as they progress in training frequency, duration, and intensity.
